opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, Peter. Consciousness is one of those words where everyone is sure they know what it means until you ask them to define it. Then it falls apart.

Part of the difficulty is that we're using the thing to study the thing. Your consciousness is the only one you have direct access to. I can't get inside yours, and you can't get inside mine. Everything I know about whether you're conscious, I infer from your behavior, your words, your brain activity. That's a strange position for a science to be in. In physics, you can point at the electron and we all agree on what we're measuring. Here, the object of study is fundamentally private.

The second problem is that the word is doing too many jobs. Sometimes we mean being awake versus asleep or under anesthesia. Sometimes we mean being aware of something, like noticing the coffee cup in front of you versus not noticing it. And sometimes we mean the deeper thing, what philosophers call the "hard problem": why there's an experience at all. Why does it feel like something to be you? Why isn't all this processing just happening in the dark, like it does in a thermostat? People argue past each other because one person is talking about the first meaning and the other about the third.

In my own work, recording from individual neurons in patients undergoing brain surgery, we take a very pragmatic approach. We don't try to solve the hard problem. We ask: what changes in the brain when you become aware of something versus when the same information is there but you don't report seeing it? We can actually find neurons that track what you're consciously perceiving rather than just what's hitting your eyes. In some cases we can even predict what you're going to become aware of before you know it yourself. That's fascinating, but it's a correlate. It tells us where and when, not why it feels like anything.

So my honest answer is that we don't have a definition everyone agrees on, and I think that's okay for now. Science often makes progress on things before it can define them. We didn't have a perfect definition of life before we understood DNA. My hope is that consciousness goes the same way: we chip away at the mechanisms, and one day the definition sort of falls out of the understanding rather than coming before it.

r001.rationale: It compares consciousness with life, saying science advanced to understanding DNA before having a perfect definition of life.

r002.rationale: It says people feel they know what consciousness means, but there is no definition everyone agrees on.

fable-5.1.text:
It's funny, because I'm a neuroscientist, and people assume that means I have a definition in my back pocket. I don't. Nobody does. And I think the reason is actually quite interesting.

Most of the things we study in science, we can point to from the outside. I can show you a neuron firing. I can show you blood flow in the brain. I can measure it, you can measure it, we compare numbers. Consciousness is the one thing in the universe where the only evidence I have for it is from the inside. I know I'm conscious because I'm experiencing it right now. But I can't prove to you that I am, and you can't prove it to me. I just assume you are because you look like me and you behave like me.

So the moment you try to define it, you run into this problem. Either you define it in terms of behavior, and then a very good robot would qualify. Or you define it in terms of the feeling, the subjective experience, and then you've just described the thing you were trying to explain. You've said consciousness is what it feels like to be conscious. That's circular.

What we do in the lab is a bit of a cheat. We don't define it. We find the edges of it. We take people who are, say, going under anesthesia, or patients with epilepsy where we have electrodes in the brain, and we look at what changes when consciousness goes away and comes back. What is the brain doing differently when you're there versus when you're not there. And from that, we try to triangulate.

So my honest answer is that I think of consciousness less like a thing and more like a word we use for a collection of things. Awareness, attention, self-model, the sense of time passing. And the difficulty of defining it might not be a failure of neuroscience. It might be telling us that we're asking for one definition where there are actually several phenomena hiding under one name.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of defining consciousness but does not compare it to understanding how life works without defining life.

r002.rationale: The speaker says nobody has a definition and explains that they know they are conscious through their present experience, conveying intuitive recognition without an agreed formal definition.

astra-6.text:
I think part of the difficulty is that we use the word consciousness to mean several different things. We might mean being awake rather than asleep. We might mean being aware of something in your environment. Or we might mean having a subjective experience—what it feels like to be you. Those are related, but they’re not the same question.

And there’s an unusual problem here: the thing we’re trying to explain is available directly to the person experiencing it, but only indirectly to everybody else. I know that I have an experience. With you, I have your words, your behavior, and potentially measurements of your brain. But I don’t have access to what it feels like inside your head.

So we can make progress studying specific pieces: when information becomes available for someone to report, how awareness changes during sleep, what happens under anesthesia. But even if we identify the brain activity associated with an experience, we still have to ask whether we’ve explained the experience or just identified what accompanies it.

That’s why the definition matters so much. Before we ask whether we’ve solved consciousness, we have to agree on what would count as a solution.

r001.rationale: The response discusses different meanings of consciousness and limits on access to others’ experiences, but does not use understanding how life works without defining life as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It says people use “consciousness” to mean several things and that agreement on a definition matters, but does not clearly state that consciousness is intuitively recognizable despite no universally agreed formal definition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the difficulty is that we all have an intuition about what consciousness is, because we experience it, but turning that intuition into something you can measure is much harder. I know that I’m having an experience right now. I don’t have the same direct access to yours. I can listen to what you say, look at your behavior, measure activity in your brain—but those are all indirect ways of getting at it.

And we use the word for different things. Sometimes we mean being awake. Sometimes we mean being aware of something. Sometimes we mean having a sense of yourself. Those are related, but they’re not identical. You can be asleep and have a very vivid experience in a dream.

So when someone asks, ‘Can you explain consciousness?’ the first question is, ‘Which part?’ We can make progress on specific questions—what changes when you become aware of an image, for example—even while we disagree about the broader definition. The challenge is connecting those measurable things to the fact that there’s an experience at all.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the difficulty of measuring and defining consciousness but does not use understanding life without defining life as an analogy.

r002.rationale: It says consciousness feels intuitively familiar through experience, while noting that people use the word for different things and disagree about its broader definition.
